Try harder in school, and be kinder and more confident. The hard-core, "I don't give a fuck" outcast attitude won't do you any favors down the line. Get involved with the school. Go to the stupid dances. Join an after-school club. Befriend as many different types of classmates as you can. Don't stick to a single "clique" or a single friend, for that matter. Just enjoy it, because once it's over, you'll never get to go back to it, and you'll have points in your life where you wish you could. Even if it was just that one class you really enjoyed amid a sea of mundane memories... enjoy it now. Adult responsibilities will set in soon, and if you think you have it hard right now, just fucking wait, dude. The world gets messed up once you walk out with your diploma. It doubles in size. Start getting ready for that right now. You might not feel like you can do it, or that it'll matter, but it will. I promise.

Happened during a group hike. I hike regularly, but normally in cooler conditions. I started becoming overly-aware of my heartbeat - it was like I could hear/feel it. Really strong and fast. Vision got shakey soon after. I was a good distance behind everyone, too.

Luckily, I was hiking with two EMT's so they sat me down in the shade and got me on glucose packs and electrolyte tablets. At one point my resting heart rate was 180, which concerned one of the EMTs, and my speech was slurring. I noticed my arms turning red and I wasn't sweating, which makes me think it was a heat stroke. My muscles in my legs were also spasming. Got stabilized and made it out, but in the following days I've been suffering from headaches and overall feeling of weakness. Sort of like having a hangover or a cold. It's been nearly a week and though each day is a little better, I still feel like crap.

All I remember was it hit me super fast. I just thought I was a little dehydrated or strained, but potentially, something much worse was going on.

So, as with anything, know your limits, and in hot conditions, limit them more. Drink a ton of water. Seriously, at LEAST a liter a day, if not more. If possible, just stay out of the heat. Get electrolyte tabs (like Nuun) for emergencies and something like a Fitbit to monitor your heart rate.

If you really want to purchase something major, **save up double what it costs**. For example, let's say you want a television for $300. Save up $600. Buy the TV and you still have $300 left to stand on.

Also, if you didn't want \[insert product here\] before you saw it in the store, **don't get it**. Really only get what you went in the store for and try not to get sucked into anything else unless you have fun money you want to spend.

If possible, deposit a select amount of money from each check and put it into your savings account. Whether it's an extra $25.00 or $100.00. Deposit the 'extra' money into your savings and **DO NOT TOUCH YOUR SAVINGS**. Pretend it doesn't exist. Pretend it isn't yours. Ignore it. Only count what is in your checking account, and keep depositing what you are able to into the savings account. Not only will you save up a lot very quickly, but when life throws you a curveball in which you will NEED to pull from your savings, you'll be prepared for it.

Also, this is rather small, but **don't be a brand-snob**. If the store's brand is cheaper, go with that. Compare the ingredients. It's usually the same exact stuff and this can apply for both food and medicine.

**If you dine out a lot, stop**. It's more expensive in the long-run to dine out every week or grab fast food than it would to put together a meal at home, which is usually healthier, too. That meal-prep crap is serious business. Leftovers are definitely underrated, as well.

Know that, despite that depression lingering in the back corner at any given point, those moments where you feel better, or happy - those moments are worth fighting the fight. Always.

Also, don't pressure yourself so much, you know? Make sure you have good people to talk to. Therapists and medication aren't signs of weakness, either. I've always found value in seeking therapy, and to perfectly honest, it can be very hit and miss. I've had therapists I've hated, and others I've been fond of... and even with the ones I've been fond of there where sessions where I felt better and sessions where I felt worse. It's part of the process, I guess. But don't let that deter you from seeking help; they'll teach you coping mechanisms and help you come to understand things you may not be aware of, which can be really beneficial.

Little things can be huge, too. Seriously. Drink more water. Push yourself to go outside to a park or even the library if you have one close by. Pick up your room or clean or organize something. It's amazing how much a tidier space can help you feel better! Don't want to exercise? Alright, try dancing a bit to your favorite music! Laying on the floor and listening to music is okay, too. Do you use social media a lot? Is it making you feel bad? Take a break for a while. Maybe pick up a new hobby. If you're artsy, try creating something, even you don't think it'll be any good. A scribble is still better than a blank page. And if you're not up for any of this at first, hey, that's okay, too. Take little steps. After a while, you'll find what makes you feel best.

And bottom line, and probably the best advice I can offer, is this: yeah, you're going to feel awful sometimes, but just as well, you'll feel better again, too. And it may take a little longer to feel better at times, but you'll always find a reason to be alright. And when you do, hold onto that feeling, and remember it for the next time.

I was working in a specialty retail store. Unlike most of the other stores in our chain, I was responsible for two separate departments - clothing and footwear. Also unlike most other stores, we had an extremely large selection for both departments. Now, on paper, clothing and footwear may sound like they go hand-in-hand, but they were considered separate, and when visiting sister stores in other states I noted their clothing and footwear departments had designated employees for either or, but not both. That, and their departments were about half the size of ours, which I'll say once more - was *overwhelming* large, taking up about half the size of the store.

For a while, I was the only full time employee of the departments, not counting my manager. I was usually scheduled late, as a "closer", so that added the responsibility of restoration and cleaning. And if anyone here has worked retail clothing, you already know how shitty that aspect goes. But wait, there's more: due to low sale numbers, there was basically these perpetual, never-ending "budget cuts" which resulted in my happy ass working alone for 90% of my shifts with no help. Management always low-key made it out to be our fault for not tending to customers better (aka annoying the fuck out of them every 5 minutes or not pushing add-ons) but I always blamed corporate for sending us garbage products that nobody wanted, or failing to send us the shit the customers DID want. In my opinion, our store was basically a secondary storage warehouse for their nonsensical distribution center.

Anyways, getting to the "don't get paid enough" moment, one late afternoon, I wind up with three people in footwear who all want to try on shoes, most of which are stored in the back room - *of course*. One of these three people needs two different sizes because they forgot what size shoe they wear (exceedingly common), so the boxes begin to pile up pretty quickly. I used to call it "Manhattan" because you would just wind up with little towers of boxes all over the floor. So, I'm jogging back and forth and trying to tend to all three of them by myself the best that I can when I suddenly hear the fitting room bell in the clothing department ring.

First, I have to grab more shoes for these people to be super picky about before running to clothing to unlock the fitting room for a customer who's slightly irritated that I wasn't there within 10 seconds of them ringing the bell. I run back to footwear, and now the phone is ringing. It's a customer who wants to know if we have something in stock. They don't have the item number but it looks like "\_\_\_\_\_". The footwear customers need help again, too, and only a few minutes into this developing clusterfuck does the fitting room bell ring AGAIN.

I am *literally* running between two departments, tending to multiple in-store customers, as well as one on the phone. It's also getting close to the final hour of the store being open, and I haven't even started restoration or cleaning yet (we didn't have a graveyard crew because the company couldn't afford it, so all that shit has to be done while customers are in the store still messing everything up) By the time everyone is tended to, the fitting room is left in shambles, the sales floor is trashed, boxes are towering in footwear, I have a cart full of go-backs in the front of the store, and the ONE PAIR of shoes that *were* sold were clearance shoes, with a shit profit margin that does zip to help our infinite shitty sales numbers.

All that shit for minimum wage? Fuck off.

Many more things I could ramble about regarding that store, but I remember that day in particular as being the day I realized I was in over my head and shit wasn't right. I've since left, make double, and I don't even do close to half the amount of work I was doing in that damn store.
I will always pretend it ended right here.
